title: Waterbeds: The Sexiest Bed?
summary: The hosts explore the history of the water bed, from Charles Hall's 1968 "pleasure pit" design student project at San Francisco State and his patented vinyl-bladder water bed, through its sexualized 1970s reputation, knockoff manufacturers, Robert Heinlein's earlier science-fiction descriptions, 19th-century hydrostatic beds for bed sores, the 1980s sales peak, the decline in the 1990s as alternative mattresses like Tempur-Pedic arrived, and modern "waveless" designs. The episode also includes a listener mail segment about red-green color blind electricians.

segments.title: Opening banter and childhood homes
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode as part of the historical pop culture series, cite The Atlantic and contemporary newspaper articles as sources, and share personal anecdotes about past water bed experiences and their childhood homes' 1970s decor.

segments.title: Charles Hall and the pleasure pit
segments.summary: Charles Hall, a San Francisco State design student, created a conversation-pit style water bed called the Pleasure Pit as his master's thesis in 1968. Newspapers covered it, and it quickly turned into a bed. Early sales spread to Bloomingdale's, hotels, and celebrities such as Hugh Hefner.

segments.title: Sexual reputation and hijacking of the idea
segments.summary: Hall intended the water bed as a pressure-free sleep revolution, but it became associated with sex in the sixties and seventies. Head shops sold early beds, knockoff makers used risqué names, and the water bed became a sitcom and movie punch line.
topics: water bed punchline in film and TV

segments.title: Early prototypes and Robert Heinlein's influence
segments.summary: Before the water bed, Hall tried a bean-bag-like chair filled with cornstarch and then Jell-O. He then used vinyl bladders filled with temperature-controlled water. Robert Heinlein's science fiction described similar beds, which complicated the patent; Hall received the patent in 1971.

segments.title: Hospital origins and 19th-century hydrostatic beds
segments.summary: Water-filled beds date back to the 1800s, when doctors designed hydrostatic beds to prevent and relieve bed sores. Heinlein had spent time in hospital beds, which inspired his descriptions.

segments.title: Hall's company, knockoffs, and patent lawsuits
segments.summary: Hall founded Inner Space Environments and opened stores selling high-end beds that did not leak. Knockoffs with poor temperature control and leaks gave water beds a bad name. Hall later pursued patent infringement suits and sold shares of a lawsuit, which raised champerty concerns.

segments.title: Industry growth, decline, and modern water beds
segments.summary: The water bed market grew into a large industry in the 1980s, with a trade association aiming to shed the sex image. Water beds were heavy and hard to move, and their popularity fell in the 1990s as alternative mattresses such as Tempur-Pedic and Sleep Number appeared. Modern designs use foam collars and spandex and are described as waveless.

segments.title: Water bed weight and moving problems
segments.summary: A filled water bed can weigh 1,500 to 2,000 pounds, needs a heavy wooden platform, and was often banned in apartment leases, especially in New York. Draining and moving them was difficult.

segments.title: Charles Hall's later inventions and closing thoughts
segments.summary: Hall later invented the solar shower. The hosts close the water bed discussion with jokes about landfills and the episode title.

segments.title: Listener mail: color blind electricians
segments.summary: A listener named James from Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, writes that two red-green color blind electricians he worked with managed to tell wire colors apart on the job, one by noticing the difference after mistakes and the other only after a co-worker asked about it.
